title: Connections still there to be data centre power
full_text:
Australia should not discount its opportunity to become a global data centre powerhouse because of the failed IPO attempt of local player Firmus Technologies, a high-profile US-based research firm says.
Margarita Patria, a Boston-based energy economist with global consultancy Charles River Associates, says Australia has key advantages in attracting data-centre investment just as rival countries such as Canada and Ireland encounter difficulties.
“Building a data centre means putting something of very significant value in one spot, so you definitely want low crime rates, a strong legal system, access to energy resources and an absence of natural disasters,” Patria says.
“With that lens, Australia is a pretty good prospect.” Patria says there is no chance that the US can fully accommodate its domestic demand for data-centre capacity without looking for offshore assistance.
“We are currently approaching the limit of what the US power grid can provide,” she says. “There is more capacity being built, but demand cannot possibly be met in the United States on the timeline that the industry wants. It’s not possible. They just want too much.
“But now Canada is becoming constrained and Mexico has its own concerns, so there are very limited options.
“Of course, there will be data centres in Europe, but those data centres are likely to serve the cloud needs of their own populations.” Patria says Australia can afford to take a measured approach. “Careful what you wish for, because they will come and data centres take a lot of energy, and people get passionate about that,” she says. “I think there is a lot of misinformation about that, but it is still a legitimate issue.’’ The global industry is still in the early stages of its development, she says. “We are still in the beginning of the demand. You see a lot of announcements but not a lot of gigawatt data centres have actually come online yet. A lot of it is still in development,” she says. “We see a lot of very serious firms making plans and contracting with utilities and providing millions of dollars in deposits and starting construction.” But she says there have also been some speculative players entering the industry – talking up their prospects – without firm backing. “We do see some new players saying: ‘We are going to build a $100bn or a trillion-dollar business’, but without much proof,” she says.
The key is the strength of any contracts that these data-centre builders have signed with hyperscalers.
“You want to see real commitments,” Patria says.
She says the key demand opportunity for Australia is in the training of large language models.
Australia’s isolation is not an obstacle when it comes to the training of so-called large language models, she says.
“With training you need significant amounts of power located in one place,” she says.
“We’re talking about gigawatts, which is very hard to find in the US. And these facilities do not have to be close to anything. You can build them far away from all the users.
“The trick is to make sure that all the data is transferred, which is very possible in Australia, and there is enough power.” Patria describes the training of AI models as being one of the three growth buckets of AI-related computing demand.
“It’s probably going to be a third of the major need because there is not just one model that’s being trained,” she says. “Many companies in the US are competing with each other with the models that they train.” This week Firmus Technologies signed its first major customer after its proposed $7bn IPO was pulled, securing a multi-year agreement with Thinking Machines Lab, the artificial-intelligence company run by former OpenAI executive Mira Murati.
Under the agreement, Thinking Machines Lab will use Firmus’s infrastructure in Asia to train and deploy its new AI models.
Firmus has also signed a deal with OpenAI, allowing the developer of the ChatGPT platform to use two new sites in Malaysia. Meta is an anchor client for one of Firmus’s sites in Batam, Indonesia, where Nvidia has underwritten capacity to on-sell to customers.
Meanwhile, shares in another local data centre operator, NextDC, on Wednesday hit a low of $5.10 after Melbourne power supply problems short-circuited the group’s earnings plans.
NextDC suffered its biggest one-day fall on record after it flagged power supply problems at its M3 Footscray centre due to community and council objections.
The company has frozen new development projects and land purchases and will review its capital spending before the annual general meeting on November 20. Stewart Oldfield is a director of industry intelligence firm Field Research.
